sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste. Berlin: Language Science Press (sec. 4.6.5 Babar, pp. 223-236).
sources.note: Nothing on Dai stress. p.224: 'The languages of the Babar node are poorly documented. The 193-item word lists in Taber (1993) are the only source of data for five of these languages: Dai [dij], North Babar [bcd], East Marsela [vme], Imroing [imr], and Tela-Masbuar [tvm].' p.226 + fn.32 quote Dai phonetic forms with Taber's stress marks ([ˈaʈʰon] 'dog', [n̩ˈnoʈ] 'run', [ˈnoʈnon] 'rattan', [ˈnɛvriʈ] 'bathe', [n̩ˈpuʈ] 'rotten', [ˈdutʔon] 'breast', [ˈmatʰʔɛˈnon] 'smoke') only for a [d]~[ʈ] allophony argument. Generic remark elsewhere (Flores chapter) that penultimate stress is the normal rule for…

sources.citation: Schapper, Antoinette & Erik Zobel. 2024. Languages of Timor and southern Maluku. Chapter 35 (pp. 567 ff., sec. 35.2.4 'Stress' p.570) in the Oxford Guide to the Malayo-Polynesian languages of Southeast Asia (A. Adelaar & A. Schapper, eds.). Oxford: OUP.
sources.note: Sec. 35.2.4 Stress (p.570), areal generalisation only: 'In the languages of Timor and also in many languages of southern Maluku (Roma, Leti, Fordata), stress is predictable and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Selaru has predictable stress which always falls on the root; if the latter is polysyllabic, the penultimate syllable is stressed.. In the languages of Aru, stress is not predictable.' Dai / the Babar languages are not mentioned in this section; no tone anywhere. NOT usable as a Dai statement.

sources.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2023a. Emplawas and languages of the Babar islands. Endangered Languages Archive deposit emplawas-edwards-0741, hdl:2196/28f40694-81ac-4d06-b515-617dd6469394.
sources.note: Deposit landing page lists 13 languages (Emplawas, Imroing, Tela-Masbuar, SE Babar, North Babar, Serili, East/West/Central Marsela, Teun, Nila, Serua, Seluwasan, Makatian); Dai is not among them, consistent with Grimes & Edwards 2026 fn.26. Nothing on Dai.

sources.citation: Zobel, Erik. 2018. The South Babar languages of Southwest Maluku. Web publication on 'Sounds from around the Pacific Ocean' (ezlinguistics.blogspot.com), last revised 20 Aug 2018 (sections: 1 Introduction, 2 Note on Taber's transcriptions, 3 Proto South Babar, 4 The position of North Babar; references).
sources.note: Nothing on Dai stress. Dai appears only in: 'PSWM.. *ʔ (only retained in Kisar, Luang and Dai)' and sec. 4.2 'In Dai and Daweloor, *u and *i were partially kept distinct and subsequently subject to fortition (*u > ʔ/k, *i > s), which is shared with West Damar.' The page's stress remarks concern the reconstruction, not any modern lect's rule: 'In stressed (= penultimate) position, all four vowels remain distinct [in Proto Southwest Maluku]'; 'consonant clusters are only allowed preceding the penultimate (= stressed) vowel' (Proto South Babar word shape); sec. 2 'Note on Taber's transcriptions'…

sources.citation: van Engelenhoven, Aone & John Hajek. 2000. East Timor and the Southwest Moluccas: language, time and connections. Studies in Languages and Cultures of East Timor 3: 106 ff. Academy of East Timor Studies, University of Western Sydney.
sources.note: No phonology content for Dai. p.109: 'Similarly, the only representative of the North Group (3700 speakers) on Babar proper is Northern Babar. The other two isolects are found respectively on Dai, Dawera and Dawelor.' The article discusses classification (Babar as a separate subgroup; Luangic-Kisaric), ethnolinguistic zones and Leti/Luang matters; its only 'stress' mention concerns Tetum Dili orthography.
sources.venue: Studies in Languages and Cultures of East Timor 3: 106 ff

sources.citation: Taber, Mark. 1999 [1993]. Toward a better understanding of the indigenous languages of Southwestern Maluku. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 1999-007. Dallas: SIL. 54 pp. (re-issue 'used by permission' of Oceanic Linguistics 32(2): 389-441, with the full Appendix 'Wordlists from the 24 languages of Southwestern Maluku', incl. the 193-item Dai list).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Read in full (extracted text, 2022 lines; a full-text search for stress/accent/penult/syllable/pitch + sec. 4.2.3.1 and notes in context). The only prosodic content is the transcription convention heading the Appendix (p.[412] of OL numbering): 'The following wordlists contain the raw phonetic data collected on survey. The symbols used here follow the International Phonetic Alphabet. Stress is marked by [ˈ].' The Dai row of the appendix carries a stress mark on every polysyllable (e.g. oiˈjon, waˈtenon, ˈnatnon, suˈʔon, raˈʔon, horˈhor) = WORDLIST-ONLY data, no statement of a rule. Dai prose…
sources.venue: Toward a better understanding of the indigenous languages of Southwestern Maluku

sources.citation: Taber, Mark (ed.). 1996. Atlas bahasa tanah Maluku. Ambon: Pusat Pengkajian dan Pengembangan Maluku, Universitas Pattimura & Summer Institute of Linguistics. xii+160 pp.

sources.citation: Taber, Mark. 1993. Toward a better understanding of the indigenous languages of Southwestern Maluku. Oceanic Linguistics 32(2): 389-441 — the 193-item Dai wordlist (Hartuti/Hertuti village) as re-keyed with Taber's stress marks in Kaiping, Edwards & Klamer (eds.) 2019, LexiRumah 3.0.0 (CLDF), lect daii1240.
sources.note: Primary data only, no prose. Every polysyllable carries a stress mark: 106 penult (ˈne-on 'sun', ˈwunn-on 'moon', ˈtakn-on 'knife', naˈnorɛn 'sea'), 63 with the mark on the last syllable (suˈʔ-on 'wind', raˈʔ-on 'blood', anˈon 'child', ɛsˈon 'person', horˈhor 'near', peˈpen 'full'; ~20 of these are verbs/adjectives like n̩ˈmat 'die', n̩ˈpuʈ 'rotten' whose only other nucleus is a syllabic nasal prefix), 1 antepenult, 5 double-marked, 18 monosyllables (tabulation). The article text itself (transcription conventions) was not accessible (JSTOR).

sources.citation: Riedel, Johan Gerard Friedrich. 1886. De sluik- en kroesharige rassen tusschen Selebes en Papua. 's-Gravenhage: Martinus Nijhoff. (Babar chapter, pp.333-334.)
sources.note: No phonology content. States that one language ('gelijk aan het literi Lagona', i.e. like Luang) is used across the islands with modified local dialects, and enumerates them (Tepasch, Manowuisch on Dai, Iliarasch, Wetolisch, Letworongsch, Kokowarisch, Anlutursch, Telaa, Imroin). Useful only for alternative names.
